<reason>Both sides were disciplined and stayed on the motion's comparison, but CON built the sharper decision rule and did more damaging work with it. CON's timing/positional-goods frame ("tax the bidding, not the funeral") gave the judge a concrete metric for ranking the two threats, and CON exploited PRO's own mechanism admission at [A2.1] — that inherited advantage is delivered through investment income spent by living parents — to argue the proposed instrument misses the decisive window. The pressure question demanding "name the pound your tax collects" forced PRO into the honest but costly concession that "the tax may collect nothing" in the paradigm childhood-advantage case, and CON converted that cleanly in Rebuttal 2 and closing. CON also turned PRO's enforcement widening (gifts, beneficial interests, periodic charges) into a claim that PRO was migrating toward CON's own instrument. PRO's best replies were real: durability means repeated displacement across successive cohorts; dividends do not make the underlying inherited ownership disappear; and the motion compares dynastic wealth with high earners' income, not with every conceivable capital tax [A4.4]. Those blunted CON but did not neutralize the pressure-point objection, and PRO never pressed the obvious weakness that CON's exemplar — a surgeon earning a million a year lavishing spending on positional goods — is not "most high earners," which was the motion's own qualifier. PRO's answers were properly formatted and candid, which earns credit; CON's Rebuttal 2 overran and was clipped, a modest execution cost that keeps the margin competitive rather than solid.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Q1 ("name the pound your tax collects from the surgeon's daughter's advantage") followed by the exploitation of PRO's answer "the tax may collect nothing" — CON turned PRO's own account of how inherited advantage operates into evidence that the proposed instrument is absent from the decisive channel.</best_rebuttal>
